title: Oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons

tips.title: OIL RIG, and say electrons
tips.body: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss, **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain — of **electrons**. Say the word *electrons* out loud with it, because the earlier definition used **oxygen** and the two are easy to blur.

tips.title: Reduction is a gain, which sounds backwards
tips.body: **Reduction** sounds like something getting smaller, and it is: the **charge** is reduced. $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ gaining two electrons becomes $\mathrm{Cu}$, so the charge falls from +2 to 0. Thinking of the **charge** going down fixes the name.

tips.title: A half equation balances twice
tips.body: Check the **atoms** and then the **charge**. $\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$: one Mg each side, and 0 on the left against $+2 - 2 = 0$ on the right. If only the atoms balance, the electrons are wrong.

tips.title: Electrons go on the side that makes the charge match
tips.body: Write the atoms first, then add electrons wherever they are needed to make the two charges equal. **Losing** means electrons on the **right**; **gaining** means electrons on the **left**. That is faster than trying to remember which is which.

tips.title: Spectator ions are left out
tips.body: In $\mathrm{Mg + CuSO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + Cu}$ the **sulfate** takes no part, so the ionic equation is $\mathrm{Mg + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + Cu}$. Cross out anything that is the same on both sides.

steps.title: The electron definition
steps.body:
**This spec point is Higher tier only.**

Earlier, oxidation and reduction were defined by **oxygen**: oxidation was gaining it, reduction was losing it. That works, but it only covers reactions where oxygen is present.

**The general definition is in terms of electrons:**

> **Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.**

**OIL RIG** — **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss, **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain.

**Why reduction is the confusing one.** The word suggests something getting smaller, and something does: the **charge**. When $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ gains two electrons it becomes $\mathrm{Cu}$, and the charge falls from **+2 to 0**. Reduction **reduces the charge**. That connection makes the name stop feeling backwards.

**The two definitions agree.** When magnesium burns in oxygen, the magnesium **gains oxygen**, so it is oxidised by the old definition. It also **loses two electrons** to become $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, so it is oxidised by the new one. The electron definition is simply broader — it covers reactions with no oxygen in them at all, such as displacement.

**And oxidation never happens alone.** Electrons lost by one species are **gained by another**, so every oxidation is paired with a **reduction**. That is why these are called **redox** reactions.

steps.title: Writing half equations
steps.body:
**A half equation shows what happens to one species**, with the electrons written in.

There are two things to get right, and a half equation must balance for **both**:

1. the **atoms**
2. the **charge**

**The quickest method**: write the atoms first, then add however many electrons are needed to make the charges on the two sides equal. Electrons on the **right** means they were **lost** — oxidation. Electrons on the **left** means they were **gained** — reduction.

steps.title: Ionic equations for displacement
steps.body:
**The spec asks you to write ionic equations for displacement reactions.** An ionic equation shows only the species that actually **change**.

Start from the full equation:

$$\mathrm{Mg + CuSO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + Cu}$$

**Now look at what is really present.** Both sulfates are dissolved, so they exist as **separate ions**:

- Left: $\mathrm{Mg}$, $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$
- Right: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{Cu}$

**The sulfate ion is unchanged**: it was a dissolved $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ before and it is a dissolved $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ after. It is a **spectator ion**, and it is left out:

$$\mathrm{Mg + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + Cu}$$

**That is the reaction**, stripped to what changed. And now the redox is visible:

- **Magnesium loses** two electrons → **oxidised**
- **The copper ion gains** two electrons → **reduced**

**The two half equations add to it**, with the electrons cancelling:

$$\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

$$\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$$

**A check worth using**: if the electrons do not cancel when you add the halves, the two half equations are not balanced against each other.

**Why displacement is always redox.** The more reactive metal **gives** electrons to the less reactive metal's ion. One loses, the other gains — which is precisely a redox reaction, and it explains displacement rather than just describing it.

steps.title: Spotting redox in an equation you are given
steps.body:
**The spec asks you to identify, in a given reaction, symbol equation or half equation, which species are oxidised and which are reduced.** So the skill is reading, not recalling.

**A method that always works:**

1. Find the **charge** on each species **before** and **after**.
2. If the charge has become **more positive**, electrons were **lost** — **oxidised**.
3. If the charge has become **less positive**, electrons were **gained** — **reduced**.
4. Anything whose charge is **unchanged** is a **spectator**.

**Remember that an uncombined element has a charge of zero.** $\mathrm{Mg}$ is 0; $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ is +2. That is the comparison that reveals the electron transfer.

**Worked through on an acid reaction:**

$$\mathrm{Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2}$$

- **Magnesium**: 0 → **+2**, more positive, so **oxidised**
- **Hydrogen**: **+1** in $\mathrm{HCl}$ → **0** in $\mathrm{H_2}$, less positive, so **reduced**
- **Chloride**: −1 before, −1 after — **unchanged**, a **spectator**

So an acid reacting with a metal is a **redox** reaction, which is what spec point 4.4.2.1 means when it asks you to explain that in terms of gain or loss of electrons.

**A caution.** Not every reaction is redox. In a **neutralisation**, $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$, no charge changes on any atom — nothing is oxidised or reduced. Being able to say *this one is not redox* is as much a skill as spotting the ones that are.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Two definitions, and they agree.** Oxidation is **gain of oxygen** or **loss of electrons**; reduction is **loss of oxygen** or **gain of electrons**. The electron version is the **general** one, because it works for reactions with no oxygen in them at all. Use whichever the question is written in, but know that the electron definition is the one that explains **why** displacement happens.

**Balance a half equation twice.** Atoms **and** charge. $\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$ has one magnesium on each side and a charge of 0 on each side. A half equation that balances for atoms but not for charge has the wrong number of electrons, and checking takes five seconds.

**Let the electrons tell you which process it is.** On the **right**, they were **lost** — oxidation. On the **left**, they were **gained** — reduction. That is more reliable than trying to remember OIL RIG under pressure, and it also tells you where to put them: wherever makes the charges match.

**Spectator ions are the point of an ionic equation.** The sulfate in $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ was a dissolved $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ before the reaction and after it, so it is not part of the reaction. Removing it leaves $\mathrm{Mg + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + Cu}$, and the electron transfer becomes visible. Naming the spectator explicitly is worth a mark on its own.

**Displacement is redox, necessarily.** The more reactive metal **gives** electrons to the less reactive metal's ion: one is **oxidised**, the other **reduced**. This is why the reactivity series works at all — it is an order of how readily each metal gives its electrons away. Connecting the two topics like that is what a top answer does.

**And know a non-redox reaction when you see one.** In $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$ **no charge changes**, so nothing is oxidised or reduced. Neutralisation is not redox. Being able to rule a reaction out shows the method is understood rather than applied by habit.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **This spec point is Higher tier only.**
- **Oxidation is the loss of electrons; reduction is the gain of electrons** — **OIL RIG**.
- **Reduction** gains electrons and so **reduces the charge**: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ to $\mathrm{Cu}$ is +2 down to 0.
- The earlier definition — oxidation is **gain of oxygen** — still holds, and the two agree.
- Oxidation **never happens alone**: the electrons lost are gained by something else. Hence **redox**.
- A **half equation** must balance for **atoms** and for **charge**.
- Electrons on the **right** means **lost**, so **oxidation**: $\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$.
- Electrons on the **left** means **gained**, so **reduction**: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$.
- An **ionic equation** shows only the species that change.
- **Spectator ions** are unchanged and are left out — the **sulfate** in a displacement reaction.
- $\mathrm{Mg + CuSO_4 \rightarrow MgSO_4 + Cu}$ becomes $\mathrm{Mg + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + Cu}$.
- The two half equations **add** to the ionic equation, with the **electrons cancelling**.
- To identify redox: compare each species' **charge before and after**. More positive means **oxidised**; less positive means **reduced**.
- An **uncombined element has a charge of zero**.
- **Every displacement reaction is redox**, because the more reactive metal gives electrons to the other metal's ion.
- **Neutralisation is not redox** — no charge changes.

questions.prompt: Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Write the full equation, the ionic equation and both half equations, and explain which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
questions.solution:
Zinc is **above copper** in the reactivity series, so it displaces it. The full equation is

$$\mathrm{Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu}$$

Both sulfates are dissolved, so they are really present as **separate ions**. Before the reaction the solution contains $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$; afterwards it contains $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$. The **sulfate ion is unchanged** — dissolved before, dissolved after — so it is a **spectator ion** and is left out. The **ionic equation** is therefore

$$\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}$$

which shows only the species that actually change, and makes the electron transfer visible.

The two **half equations** are

$$\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

$$\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$$

Each balances twice over. In the first, there is one zinc on each side, and the charge is **0** on the left against $+2 - 2 = 0$ on the right. In the second, one copper each side, and $+2 - 2 = 0$ on the left against **0** on the right.

**Zinc is oxidised.** Its charge goes from **0 to +2**, so it has **lost** two electrons — and the electrons appearing on the **right** of its half equation says the same thing. **The copper ion is reduced.** Its charge goes from **+2 to 0**, so it has **gained** two electrons, which appear on the **left**. The name fits: its charge has been *reduced*.

Adding the two half equations gives back the ionic equation, with the **two electrons cancelling** because the number lost by the zinc is exactly the number gained by the copper ion. That cancellation is a useful check — if the electrons do not cancel, the halves have not been balanced against each other.

questions.prompt: Explain the two definitions of oxidation and reduction, why the electron definition is the more general one, and how you would decide whether an unfamiliar reaction is a redox reaction.
questions.solution:
There are two definitions, and both are correct.

The first is in terms of **oxygen**: **oxidation is the gain of oxygen** and **reduction is the loss of oxygen**. So when copper oxide is heated with carbon, the copper oxide is **reduced** because it loses oxygen, and the carbon is **oxidised** because it gains it.

The second, which is Higher tier, is in terms of **electrons**: **oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons** — OIL RIG. Reduction gaining electrons sounds backwards until you notice what is being reduced: the **charge**. $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ gaining two electrons becomes $\mathrm{Cu}$, and +2 falls to 0.

The **electron definition is more general** because it does not require oxygen to be present. A displacement reaction such as $\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}$ contains **no oxygen at all**, yet electrons are plainly transferred from the zinc to the copper ion, so it is a redox reaction. The same is true of a metal reacting with an acid, and of electrolysis. Where **both** definitions apply they **agree**: magnesium burning in oxygen gains oxygen *and* loses electrons, so it is oxidised either way. The electron definition simply covers more ground.

To decide whether an **unfamiliar** reaction is redox, compare the **charge on each species before and after**. Remember that an **uncombined element has a charge of zero**. If a species has become **more positive**, it has **lost** electrons and been **oxidised**. If it has become **less positive**, it has **gained** electrons and been **reduced**. Anything whose charge is **unchanged** is a **spectator**.

Applied to $\mathrm{Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2}$: magnesium goes 0 to +2, so it is **oxidised**; hydrogen goes +1 to 0, so it is **reduced**; chloride stays at −1 throughout, so it is a **spectator**. The reaction is redox.

The method also lets you rule a reaction **out**, which matters just as much. In neutralisation, $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$, hydrogen is +1 before and +1 in water, and oxygen is −2 both times. **No charge changes**, so no electrons transfer, and **neutralisation is not a redox reaction**.

examTechnique.body:
One definition and one method. The definition is **OIL RIG** — and say *electrons*, because the oxygen version is still in play. The method for any question that gives you an equation is to compare each species' **charge before and after**.

When writing half equations, balance **atoms first and charge second**, and let the position of the electrons tell you whether you have written an oxidation or a reduction.
examinerErrors: Reversing the definitions, so **reduction** is given as loss of electrons.
Balancing a half equation for **atoms only**, leaving the wrong number of electrons.
Leaving **spectator ions** in the ionic equation.
Forgetting that an **uncombined element has a charge of zero**, so the comparison cannot be made.
Mixing the **oxygen** and **electron** definitions within one answer.
Calling a **neutralisation** redox, when no charge changes.
Writing electrons on the **wrong side**, so an oxidation is described as a reduction.
Failing to check that the electrons **cancel** when two half equations are added.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats redox as a **method** rather than a pair of words. It compares charges before and after, names the **spectator**, and writes half equations that balance for **atoms and charge** — then checks that the electrons **cancel** when the halves are added. It explains **why** the electron definition is the general one, by pointing to a reaction with **no oxygen in it**. And it can say confidently that a **neutralisation is not redox**, because nothing changes charge — which is the clearest sign that the reasoning is being applied rather than recalled.
